summary: This memo describes an implementation of the Exterior Gateway Protocol for Berkeley UNIX 4.2. It is a status report that also discusses possible extensions and design issues, as an invitation for further discussion.

eli5.summary: Someone built a router program on a UNIX computer and wrote down how it went, plus ideas for making it better.

questions: how was egp implemented on berkeley unix
subtitle: Implementing exterior routing on Berkeley UNIX 4.2 systems

tldr.problem: Internet gateways needed a protocol to exchange routing information across autonomous systems, but existing approaches were static and did not work when the core gateway system transitioned to dynamic routing via the Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP).
tldr.mechanism: This memo describes an implementation of EGP for Berkeley UNIX 4.2, running as a user-level process that maintains routing tables, acquires and monitors neighboring gateways, and exchanges network reachability information via Hello, Poll and Update messages.
tldr.outcome: The implementation demonstrated that EGP could run on commercial UNIX systems without kernel modifications, enabling organizations like ISI to add backup gateway capability and participate in the Internet's dynamic routing infrastructure.

today: RFC 911 is a historic document describing an experimental EGP implementation from 1984. EGP itself has been superseded by Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) for Internet routing. However, this RFC is historically significant as it documented the first practical implementation of EGP on commercial operating systems and demonstrated how dynamic routing protocols could run as user-level processes rather than requiring kernel modifications.

sections.title: EGP Implementation on UNIX
sections.content:
RFC 911 describes an implementation of the Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) running on Berkeley UNIX 4.2, a commercially available operating system. EGP allows gateways in different autonomous systems (AS)—independent networks managed by different organizations—to exchange routing information about which networks are reachable through them.

The Internet architecture was evolving toward a two-tier system: a core AS of gateways maintained by BBN that acts as a hub, and many stub ASs managed by other organizations that connect to the core. Before August 1984, non-routing gateways did not need EGP and had static entries in core routing tables, but that changed. The ISI (Information Sciences Institute) had a non-routing gateway to UC Irvine's network and wanted both a way to advertise it dynamically and a backup gateway in case their main connection went down. Since 23 of the 28 existing non-routing gateways were UNIX systems, building an EGP implementation for UNIX 4.2 was a clear need.
sections.eli5: The Internet was getting bigger and needed each organization's routers to tell the main routers about their networks. Someone wrote the code to do that on regular UNIX computers.

sections.title: Gateway Design and Routing Tables
sections.content:
The implementation splits routing functions between kernel and user process. The kernel handles the performance-critical job of forwarding packets using its fast routing tables. EGP and route updates run as a user-level process, similar to Berkeley's routed daemon, which makes the system easier to develop and distribute since the kernel needs only minor changes.

The EGP process maintains two sets of routing tables: one for routes to networks outside the local AS (exterior routes learned via EGP) and one for interior routes within the local AS. This separation lets the gateway prepare outgoing EGP updates containing only interior routing information. The process keeps kernel routing tables consistent by listening for ICMP redirect messages on a raw socket and updating its tables accordingly. At startup, it reads the kernel memory to copy the kernel's current routes into the EGP process tables, ensuring consistency.
sections.eli5: The router has two sets of route tables: one for how to get to distant networks and one for nearby networks. The main part of the computer routes packets quickly, and a helper program keeps track of the route information.

sections.title: Neighbor Acquisition and Reachability
sections.content:
EGP uses a three-step process with neighbor gateways. First, neighbor acquisition is a two-way handshake in which gateways exchange Request and Confirm messages including minimum Hello and Poll intervals. Trusted neighbor addresses are configured in an initialization file; the gateway only accepts acquisitions from trusted neighbors and enforces a maximum number of simultaneously acquired neighbors.

Second, neighbor reachability is maintained by periodically sending Hello commands and receiving I-H-U (I Heard You) responses to confirm each gateway is up and reachable. A shift register tracks responses: if a neighbor loses reachability (≤1 of the last 4 responses received), routes through it are deleted. Third, network reachability is determined by periodically sending Poll commands and receiving Update responses listing the networks reachable via one or more gateways. Routes are aged out if not refreshed within 4 minutes or 3 times the maximum poll interval. The implementation also monitors sequence numbers to handle message ordering and resends Polls if Updates are not received for three successive polls.
sections.eli5: The routers shake hands to agree to talk, they say hello to check if each other is still working, and they regularly swap lists of networks they can reach.

sections.title: Topology Management and Routing Loops
sections.content:
A critical issue is preventing routing loops—situations where two gateways point to each other for the same destination, creating a cycle. EGP itself does not prevent loops; it only enables neighbors to exchange information. The implementation initially proposed restricting the network topology to a tree structure to prevent alternate routes via different autonomous systems. However, a more flexible interim model emerged: gateways use conflict resolution rules when network reachability reports conflict—directly connected networks take precedence over interior routes, interior routes take precedence over exterior routes, and the latest received report takes precedence.

The ISI gateway configuration exemplifies these issues. ISI-Hobgoblin (a VAX 11/750 running this EGP implementation) could provide backup gateway capability to ISI-GATEWAY between ARPANET and ISI-NET, but the existence of two potential paths creates a routing loop risk. The implementation prevents this by ensuring that ISI-Hobgoblin and ISI-GATEWAY do not simultaneously conduct EGP over both ARPANET and ISI-NET, so they cannot learn about alternate routes and create a loop.
sections.eli5: Multiple routers could accidentally create circles in routing instructions, so the implementation carefully controls which routers talk to which others to prevent that.

sections.title: Implementation Lessons
sections.content: Testing revealed several important issues. Different implementers interpreted the original EGP specification's narrative description of sequence numbers inconsistently, causing gateways to incorrectly reject messages. The RFC editor's more formal specification in RFC 1745 (referenced as Mills 84a) eliminated these ambiguities. Another issue: when both gateways sent Error responses for invalid interfaces before checking the message type, they created loops. The implementation fixed this by not sending Error responses to Error messages. A third problem occurred when a core gateway sent malformed EGP Updates: the implementation could time out all routes. The solution was to count successive Polls without valid Updates and cease EGP after 3 failures to acquire an alternative gateway.
sections.eli5: The writers of the original rules didn't think through all the corner cases, so the team that built this found and fixed confusing situations.
